title: Butter vs. Olive Oil: Fat, Calories, and Key Differences

seo.title: Butter vs. Olive Oil: Fat, Calories, and Differences
seo.meta_description: A tablespoon of butter has about 102 calories and 7 g saturated fat; olive oil about 119 calories and 2 g saturated fat, with far more monounsaturated fat.
seo.search_intent: Compare butter and olive oil for calories, saturated fat, monounsaturated fat, and cooking use.

excerpt: Olive oil is slightly higher in calories by tablespoon because it is essentially all fat, while butter contains water. Their fatty-acid profiles differ much more: a tablespoon of butter has about 7 g saturated fat, compared with roughly 2 g in olive oil, where monounsaturated oleic acid dominates.
content_html:
Butter and olive oil are both cooking fats, but they are not nutritionally interchangeable. The biggest difference is not whether they contain fat—it is which fats dominate and how much water is present.

Per-tablespoon comparison

Butter ~14 gOlive oil ~13.5 g
Calories~102~119
Total fat~11.5 g~13.5 g
Saturated fat~7.3 g~1.9 g
Monounsaturated fat~3 g~10 g

Olive oil is more calorie-dense because it is almost pure fat. Butter contains roughly 15–18% water.

The fatty-acid profile is where they separate

Butter is rich in saturated fat. Olive oil is dominated by oleic acid, a monounsaturated fat. U.S. heart-health guidance generally recommends replacing some saturated fat with unsaturated fats rather than simply adding more total fat.

Butter is not “forbidden”

A nutrition comparison does not require turning one food into poison and the other into medicine. Amount and frequency matter. Butter can fit in a diet, while olive oil generally offers a more favorable fatty-acid profile when used as a routine cooking fat.

A tablespoon is closer to the everyday comparison

Butter and oil are concentrated fats, but butter contains some water while oil is almost entirely fat. Per 100 g, oil can therefore look even more calorie-dense; the more meaningful nutritional difference is mainly the fatty-acid profile. At tablespoon scale, portion size and how much is actually used can matter as much as the per-100-gram number.

They behave differently in cooking

Butter contains milk solids that brown and create flavor but can burn at higher heat. Olive oil lacks those solids and works across dressings, sautéing, roasting, and many frying applications.

Calories are fairly close per spoonful; saturated versus unsaturated fat is the more meaningful nutritional difference.

Choosing the fat by dish, not by a single number

Butter and olive oil behave differently because butter is an emulsion containing water and milk solids, while olive oil is essentially pure fat. The water in butter evaporates during cooking and the milk solids can brown, producing nutty flavors that olive oil cannot reproduce. Extra-virgin olive oil, in contrast, contributes its own fruitiness, bitterness, and peppery notes. Those sensory differences often matter more to a recipe than the small calorie gap created by tablespoon measurements.

For sautéing vegetables, fish, eggs, or aromatics, extra-virgin olive oil works well at ordinary home-cooking temperatures. Butter is useful when browning and dairy flavor are desired, but its milk solids can darken if heat is aggressive. Clarified butter removes most water and milk solids and therefore behaves differently from whole butter. Treating all three as interchangeable simply because they are cooking fats misses both flavor and heat behavior.

Fatty-acid composition is the more important nutritional contrast. Olive oil is dominated by monounsaturated fat, whereas butter contains a much larger proportion of saturated fat. Major cardiovascular guidance recommends replacing sources of saturated fat with unsaturated fats rather than merely adding extra oil on top of an unchanged diet. In practice, that can mean using olive oil more often for everyday cooking while keeping butter where its particular flavor or baking function is valuable.

Baking is one area where substitution needs recipe-specific judgment. Butter contributes solid fat, water, milk solids, and aeration properties that affect cookies, cakes, laminated doughs, and pastry. Liquid olive oil cannot always replace it cup-for-cup without changing texture. In recipes designed for oil, however, olive oil can provide moisture and tenderness very effectively. Nutritional comparisons should not be separated from the chemistry that makes a recipe work.

Portion size remains relevant for both. A generous free-pour of olive oil can add more calories than a measured pat of butter even though its fatty-acid profile is generally more favorable. If energy intake matters, measure the amount used in dressings or pans rather than assuming a “healthy oil” is calorie-free. The practical hierarchy is therefore nuanced: prefer unsaturated oils for much of routine cooking, use butter selectively for flavor or function, and keep the quantity visible.

There is also no requirement to choose only one fat for a recipe. A small amount of butter can be paired with olive oil when both browned-milk flavor and olive character are wanted, provided the total amount still suits the dish. Thinking in terms of function, fatty-acid profile, and quantity produces a more useful decision than labeling one ingredient categorically good and the other bad.

faq.question: Which has more calories, butter or olive oil?
faq.answer: Olive oil usually has slightly more per tablespoon, about 119 versus 102 calories, because it is nearly pure fat.

faq.question: Which has more saturated fat?
faq.answer: Butter, at roughly 7 g per tablespoon versus about 2 g in olive oil.

faq.question: Can you cook with olive oil?
faq.answer: Yes. It works for dressings, sautéing, roasting, and many frying uses when temperature is controlled appropriately.
